story.title: Why should a token become permanent as soon as it is generated?
paragraphs: Autoregressive decoding commits to each token from left to right; when a later phrase makes an earlier choice look wrong, revising it takes another sequential pass. Parallel decoding cuts latency, but independently proposed tokens can disagree. COrAL keeps the sequential structure while making nearby predictions revisable.

The key restriction is locality: COrAL learns dependencies only within a bounded window, not arbitrary orderings over a whole sequence. A position can be predicted from the prefix or reconstructed with some later text visible, and agreement between these two views helps decide what to keep.

mechanism.title: Train for revision, then decode with several views of each position
paragraphs: Forward training predicts several future positions from clean sequences. Reconstruction training corrupts patches by replacement or repetition and asks the model to recover the original tokens. Refinement is therefore a trained capability, not an instruction given to an unchanged next-token model.

To predict several positions from one context, COrAL applies a generalized RoPE (rotary position embedding) in the last Transformer layer so that the query encodes the target position, avoiding a separate output head for each offset. Training adapts the last layer first and then the whole network, to limit the mismatch with the pretrained model.

At inference, a sliding block holds the positions to predict or revise. The model combines conditional distributions weighted by dependency distance and confidence, builds candidate blocks, and verifies them with next-token and backward probabilities plus a contrastive term. Only the accepted prefix is committed and advances the window; other positions stay revisable.

evidence.title: Full COrAL gains on three of five benchmarks and fails on code
paragraphs: Among COrAL’s settings, backward refinement without multi-forward prediction gives the highest accuracy and the lowest throughput, and multi-forward prediction without verification the highest throughput and the lowest accuracy; the full method lies between them on every benchmark. The abstract’s 4.6-point GSM8K gain and 3.9× speedup thus come from two different settings. Throughput is accepted tokens per second, measured for both decoders without a KV cache at batch size 1.

Code is the boundary. The paper attributes the HumanEval drop mainly to invalid syntax; recovering most of the pass rate requires turning off multi-forward prediction and raising the acceptance threshold, which runs slower than the baseline. Local agreement helps refinement but does not ensure well-formed programs.
